title: The US Struck Iran Over the Weekend. Iran Hit Back at a US Base in Kuwait. The Ceasefire Is Fraying.
excerpt: Kuwait's air defenses intercepted missiles and drones on Monday morning as the three-month-old war produced its latest exchange of fire — even as both sides say a deal is close.
body:
The United States struck Iranian military sites on the Gulf coast over the weekend. Hours later, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had targeted a US air base in retaliation. On Monday morning, air defense sirens sounded across Kuwait as the country's military intercepted incoming missiles and drones.

The exchange — the latest in a pattern of sporadic strikes since an April ceasefire — is the starkest reminder yet that the three-month-old US-Iran war is not over, and that the deal both sides say is close remains frustratingly elusive.

## What Happened

US Central Command said its fighter aircraft struck **Iranian air defenses, a ground control station, and two one-way attack drones** on Iran's Qeshm Island and Goruk in Hormozgan province, after Iran shot down an American MQ-1 surveillance drone operating over international waters.

"U.S. fighter aircraft swiftly responded by eliminating Iranian air defences that posed clear threats to ships transiting regional waters," CENTCOM said in a post on X. The strikes were described as defensive.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responded by targeting what it called "an air base used by the US for an attack on southern Iran." The IRGC did not identify the base, but Kuwait — home to a major US military installation — confirmed it came under attack.

The Kuwait Army said its air defense systems were "currently responding to hostile missile and drone threats" and that **explosions heard across the country were from intercepted missiles**. Five US service members were injured in a separate Iranian missile strike on a Kuwaiti airbase on Saturday, according to reports.

## A Ceasefire in Name Only

The ceasefire that took effect in early April was supposed to create space for negotiations. Instead, both sides have exchanged strikes at least three times in the past week alone. Last Thursday saw a nearly identical sequence: a US drone was shot down, the US struck back, Iran retaliated.

The Wall Street Journal reported that the US and Iran are discussing a memorandum of understanding that would lift blockages in the Strait of Hormuz, extend the ceasefire, and create a 60-day window to resolve the nuclear question and sanctions relief.

President Trump, speaking on Fox News on Saturday, said Iran had agreed not to develop or acquire nuclear weapons — "a big difference" from earlier positions. But he also warned that if terms are not met, "we're going to end it a different way." Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth added that 50,000 US troops remain in the region, "more than capable" of resuming full-scale operations.

Iran's lead negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, responded on Sunday that no deal would be signed unless Iranian rights are protected.

## The Oil Price Roller Coaster

Markets are whipsawing on every headline. Last week, Brent crude dropped more than 11 percent — its sharpest weekly loss since April — on hopes that a peace deal would reopen the Strait of Hormuz. On Monday, prices bounced back: WTI rose 2.5 percent to $89.60 and Brent climbed 2.2 percent to $93.16 after the weekend strikes shattered the optimism.

"Market participants seem eager to price in a resolution, but a potential deal remains elusive after seven weeks of negotiations," Barclays commodities analyst Amarpreet Singh wrote in a note.

The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed. While a few tankers have made the transit in recent weeks, several have come under attack, underscoring the risks for ship owners. Approximately 15 million barrels per day of the world's oil supply normally passes through the waterway.

## What India Is Watching

For India, the stakes could not be higher. As the world's third-largest oil consumer and a country that historically sourced over 60 percent of its crude from the Gulf, every escalation in the Hormuz corridor has direct economic consequences.

The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee meets this week to decide on interest rates, with oil prices, the weakening rupee, and a forecasted weak monsoon all complicating the calculus. India's forex reserves have fallen $47 billion in three months as the central bank defends the currency.

Indian refiners have already begun pivoting imports to Latin America and Africa, but the diversification takes time. A sustained failure of the deal would mean more pain — for domestic fuel prices, for inflation, and for the millions of NRIs whose remittances lose value as the rupee weakens.

The coming days will determine whether the memorandum of understanding can hold, or whether the world's most important shipping lane stays shut through the summer.

*Sources: Reuters, Wall Street Journal, CENTCOM (via X), Kuwait Army statement (KUNA), Barclays Research, Fox News, The Business Standard*
author: Diaspora Desk
